author: Morgan Reddekopp; reporting with Kirsten Swanson
title: Minnesota won $90 million in judgments against Medicaid fraudsters. Only a fraction is actually paid back.
notes: 5 INVESTIGATES analysis of Minnesota state court records, not merely a restatement of an agency press release. Quotes the Attorney General's chief of staff directly on collection responsibility. dateModified per page metadata is 2026-08-04T14:22:38Z.
supports: Since 2019, Minnesota's Medicaid Fraud Control Unit (MFCU) has secured more than 340 convictions and the Attorney General's office states MFCU has won $90 million in judgments and recoveries.
The $90 million figure is composed of criminal restitution ordered in MFCU-prosecuted cases plus civil settlements/judgments ordered by courts; it is not a cash-collected total.
Since 2019, judges have ordered defendants to pay back nearly $32 million in restitution in MFCU-prosecuted cases.
As of May (2026 per corpus context), the amount recorded as paid back in the state court system was just over $3 million, roughly a 9% collection rate against the $32 million ordered.
The Attorney General's office states it separately counts roughly $61 million in civil judgments; a KSTP request to DHS to substantiate/break down that figure was still pending as of publication.
The Attorney General's chief of staff stated the AG's office plays no role in collecting restitution, characterizing collection as the role of the probation system and the courts.

The article states Minnesota law does not allow the state to seize assets from convicted fraudsters, contrasted with federal authorities' reported recovery of $60-70 million in cash and assets in the Feeding Our Future investigation.

system_metrics.notes: Reported collection rate ~9% of the $32M ordered. Exact May date not specified beyond the month.

Attributed to the AG's office; DHS confirmation/breakdown request was pending at publication. Note $32M + $61M = $93M, not exactly the $90M headline figure; treat as an unresolved rounding/component discrepancy, not reconciled here.

does_not_support: That the $32M ordered and the $61M civil judgments are cleanly non-overlapping components that sum to exactly $90M; the arithmetic does not match the AG's own headline and the discrepancy is unexplained in this source.
Any case-by-case or year-by-year breakdown of who paid what; the source gives only the aggregate figures.
That the 9% collection rate applies to the $61M civil-judgment component; the article's collection-rate reporting is specific to the $32M criminal-restitution component only.
